title: Electricity and Magnetism I
subject: Physics

cards.prompt: What is Electric Charge? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Electric charge is a signed property of matter that determines electromagnetic interaction. Positive and negative charges can cancel in a net total, while zero net charge does not imply absence of charged constituents.
required_concepts: Signed electromagnetic source property.
Neutrality concerns net charge.
major_error_concepts: Assuming an electrically neutral object contains no charged particles.

cards.prompt: What is Charge Conservation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Charge conservation means the net electric charge of an isolated system remains constant. Charge can move across a system boundary or be redistributed internally, but the accounting must include all participating charges.
required_concepts: Isolated-system net charge is conserved.
major_error_concepts: Calling redistribution of charge creation of net charge.

cards.prompt: What is Charge Quantization? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In ordinary matter, net charge changes through transfers of particles carrying discrete charges, commonly integer multiples of the elementary charge e for isolated everyday objects. Continuous charge densities are useful macroscopic approximations to this discrete structure.
required_concepts: Discrete elementary charge transfers underlie macroscopic charge.
Density approximation does not remove microscopic discreteness.
accepted_variants: Charge quantization in ordinary macroscopic matter.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting a continuous density model as proof that individual electrons carry arbitrary fractions of e.

cards.prompt: What is Conductor? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A conductor contains charges able to move over macroscopic distances in response to an electric field. Their redistribution can reach electrostatic equilibrium, but conductivity does not mean that every current-carrying conductor has zero internal field.
required_concepts: Mobile charge carriers.
Electrostatic and current-carrying conditions differ.
major_error_concepts: Claiming electric field must vanish inside every resistive wire carrying steady current.

cards.prompt: What is Insulator? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An insulator strongly limits long-range charge transport under the stated conditions. Its bound charges can still shift or orient locally, so an insulator can polarize and respond to electric fields.
required_concepts: Limited macroscopic charge mobility.
Local polarization remains possible.
major_error_concepts: Assuming an insulator cannot respond electrically because charges cannot flow freely across it.

cards.prompt: What is Electrostatic Induction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Electrostatic induction redistributes mobile charge in a conductor in response to nearby charge without requiring direct contact. Net charge transfer requires a conducting path or another transfer mechanism; redistribution alone preserves the conductor's total charge.
required_concepts: Nearby charge induces redistribution.
Redistribution alone does not change net charge.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every induced charge separation automatically changes total charge.

cards.prompt: What is Coulomb Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Coulomb's law gives the electrostatic force between point charges in vacuum as magnitude |q_1 q_2|/(4pi epsilon_0 r squared). It acts along their separation, repelling equal signs and attracting opposite signs; extended distributions require superposition.
required_concepts: Inverse-square point-charge force with sign-dependent attraction or repulsion.
major_error_concepts: Using the distance between arbitrary centers for any extended charge distribution without symmetry or approximation.

cards.prompt: What is Electric Superposition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Electric-force superposition means the total force on a test charge is the vector sum of forces from the source charges in the classical model. Magnitudes alone cannot generally be added because directions matter.
required_concepts: Vector sum of individual contributions.
major_error_concepts: Adding force magnitudes without accounting for directions.

cards.prompt: What is Electric Field? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The electric field is force per unit positive test charge, E=F/q, with the test charge small enough not to alter the source configuration in the defining limit. Field direction is the force direction for positive charge.
required_concepts: Force per unit positive test charge.
Source disturbance excluded in definition.
major_error_concepts: Defining field direction using the force on a negative charge without reversing it.

cards.prompt: What is Point-Charge Field? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A point charge q at the origin produces E=q r_hat/(4pi epsilon_0 r squared) away from the source point. The sign sets inward or outward direction, and the formula is singular at the idealized point charge.
required_concepts: Radial inverse-square field with source-charge sign.
major_error_concepts: Assigning a finite self-field at the point charge using the ordinary r=0 formula.

cards.prompt: What is Continuous Charge Field? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A continuous charge distribution produces a field found by integrating point-charge contributions over source locations. The displacement vector runs from each source element to the observation point, not the reverse.
required_concepts: Integrate vector contributions from source elements.
Source-to-observer displacement convention.
major_error_concepts: Using one constant source distance across an extended distribution without justification.

cards.prompt: What is Linear Charge Density? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Linear charge density lambda is charge per unit source length, giving dq=lambda dl. It can vary along the line and has units of charge divided by length.
required_concepts: Charge per length with dq=lambda dl.
major_error_concepts: Using line density as charge per surface area.

cards.prompt: What is Surface Charge Density? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Surface charge density sigma is charge per unit area, giving dq=sigma dA. It describes charge concentrated on a surface and may vary with position, especially near edges or curved conductor regions.
required_concepts: Charge per area with dq=sigma dA.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every conductor surface must have uniform charge density regardless of shape.

cards.prompt: What is Volume Charge Density? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Volume charge density rho is charge per unit volume, giving dq=rho dV. Integrating it over a region gives net enclosed volume charge, with separate surface or point contributions included when present.
required_concepts: Charge per volume and volume integration.
major_error_concepts: Ignoring surface-charge contributions while claiming a volume-density integral contains every possible source.

cards.prompt: What is Electric Field Lines? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Electric field lines are curves tangent to the electric field at each point, oriented as a positive charge's force direction. Their plotted density can illustrate strength, but the lines are a visualization rather than physical trajectories a charge must follow.
required_concepts: Tangent-direction representation of the field.
Not generally particle trajectories.
major_error_concepts: Assuming an inertial charged particle must move exactly along a field line regardless of its velocity.

cards.prompt: What is Electric Flux? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Electric flux through an oriented surface is the integral of E dot n dA. It counts the normal field contribution with sign and can vanish despite a nonzero field tangent to the surface or canceling contributions.
required_concepts: Oriented normal field integral.
major_error_concepts: Concluding zero net flux implies zero electric field everywhere on the surface.

cards.prompt: What is Gauss Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Gauss's law states that electric flux through a closed surface equals enclosed net charge divided by epsilon_0 in vacuum, with all charge included. External charges can affect the field on the surface but contribute zero net enclosed-source flux.
required_concepts: Closed electric flux equals Q_enclosed/epsilon_0.
External sources can still affect local field.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the electric field on a Gaussian surface depends only on enclosed charge in every geometry.

cards.prompt: What is Gaussian Surface and Symmetry? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A Gaussian surface is an imaginary closed integration surface used in Gauss's law. Symmetry must justify extracting a constant field magnitude or eliminating components; the law itself holds without that simplifying symmetry.
required_concepts: Imaginary closed flux surface.
Symmetry is needed for easy field extraction, not for the law's validity.
major_error_concepts: Solving E times area=Q/epsilon_0 for an arbitrary surface with nonuniform field.

cards.prompt: What is Spherical Charge Field? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A spherically symmetric charge distribution has a radial field with magnitude determined by enclosed charge at each radius: E_r=Q_enclosed(r)/(4pi epsilon_0 r squared). Exterior behavior matches a point charge, while interior behavior depends on the distribution.
required_concepts: Radial field from enclosed charge at radius r.
major_error_concepts: Using total charge instead of enclosed charge inside every spherical distribution.

cards.prompt: What is Infinite Sheet Field? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ideal infinite uniformly charged sheet in vacuum produces field magnitude |sigma|/(2epsilon_0) on each side, directed away for positive charge. A conductor-surface field formula can differ because the conditions on the opposite side differ.
required_concepts: Infinite isolated sheet field sigma/(2epsilon_0).
Distinguish sheet model from conductor boundary.
major_error_concepts: Using sigma/epsilon_0 for an isolated nonconducting sheet without another field contribution.

cards.prompt: What is Infinite Line Field? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ideal infinite straight line of charge has radial cylindrical field E_r=lambda/(2pi epsilon_0 r). The result follows from translational and rotational symmetry and is an approximation for long finite lines away from their ends.
required_concepts: Cylindrical inverse-distance line field.
major_error_concepts: Using the point-charge inverse-square law for the field of an infinite uniform line.

cards.prompt: What is Electric Potential? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Electric potential in electrostatics is potential energy per unit charge relative to a chosen reference. It is a scalar, and only differences affect the work on a charge when the reference is shifted uniformly.
required_concepts: Potential energy per charge with reference freedom.
major_error_concepts: Confusing potential, measured in energy per charge, with electric field, measured in force per charge.

cards.prompt: What is Potential Difference? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For an electrostatic field, V(b)-V(a)=-integral from a to b of E dot dl. The field points toward decreasing potential, and path independence requires the electrostatic conservative-field conditions on the relevant domain.
required_concepts: Potential difference is negative line integral of field.
major_error_concepts: Using a positive field integral for V_final-V_initial without changing convention.

cards.prompt: What is Point-Charge Potential? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: With potential zero at infinity, a point charge produces V=q/(4pi epsilon_0 r). Unlike the field magnitude, the potential scales inversely with distance and retains the sign of the charge.
required_concepts: Signed inverse-distance point potential.
major_error_concepts: Using inverse-square distance for point-charge potential.

cards.prompt: What is Potential Superposition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Electrostatic potentials from multiple sources add as scalars when a consistent reference is used. A continuous distribution gives V=integral dq/(4pi epsilon_0 R) where that reference and integral are meaningful.
required_concepts: Scalar sum with consistent reference.
major_error_concepts: Adding potential magnitudes while discarding charge signs.

cards.prompt: What is Field-Potential Relation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An electrostatic field is E=-gradient V. Its components are negative spatial derivatives of potential, and a constant potential region has zero field where the differentiability assumptions hold.
required_concepts: Electric field is negative potential gradient.
major_error_concepts: Taking the field to be V divided by distance in every nonuniform geometry instead of a derivative.

cards.prompt: What is Equipotential? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An equipotential is a set of points with equal electric potential. In electrostatics the field is normal to a smooth equipotential where nonzero, and moving a charge along it changes no electrostatic potential energy.
required_concepts: Constant-potential set and zero tangential field.
major_error_concepts: Claiming zero work along an equipotential means the normal electric field must also vanish.

cards.prompt: What is Electrostatic Potential Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For point charges assembled electrostatically, interaction energy is the sum over distinct pairs of q_i q_j/(4pi epsilon_0 r_ij). Counting each pair once avoids double counting and excludes the divergent ideal point self-energies.
required_concepts: Pairwise interaction energy counted once.
major_error_concepts: Summing every ordered pair without the compensating one-half factor.

cards.prompt: What is Electric Dipole? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An electric dipole consists of equal opposite charges separated by a displacement, with dipole moment p=q d directed from negative to positive charge. The ideal dipole approximation describes distances much larger than the separation.
required_concepts: Moment points negative to positive.
Far-distance dipole approximation.
major_error_concepts: Defining dipole moment from positive to negative without changing sign conventions.

cards.prompt: What is Dipole Far Field? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Far from a localized ideal electric dipole, potential scales as 1/r squared and electric field as 1/r cubed, with angular dependence. Zero net charge removes the monopole term but does not make the distant field identically zero.
required_concepts: Dipole far-field scaling with angular dependence.
major_error_concepts: Assuming equal opposite source charges cancel the field at every observation point.

cards.prompt: What is Electric Dipole Torque? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A dipole in a uniform external electric field experiences torque tau=p cross E. The net force is zero in the ideal uniform-field case, while a nonuniform field can also exert a net force.
required_concepts: Dipole alignment torque p cross E.
Uniform-field net force distinction.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a dipole must have a nonzero net force in every uniform electric field.

cards.prompt: What is Electric Dipole Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A permanent electric dipole in a prescribed uniform external field has orientation energy U=-p dot E up to a constant. Alignment lowers energy; induced dipoles require care because the moment itself depends on the field.
required_concepts: Orientation energy minus p dot E for a fixed dipole.
major_error_concepts: Using the permanent fixed-dipole formula without accounting for the work of inducing a changing moment.

cards.prompt: What is Conductor Electrostatic Equilibrium? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Inside the material of an ideal conductor in electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field vanishes and potential is constant on each connected conductor. This equilibrium condition does not describe resistive conductors sustaining a current.
required_concepts: Zero internal electrostatic field and constant connected-conductor potential.
major_error_concepts: Applying zero internal field to every steady resistive current situation.

cards.prompt: What is Conductor Surface Field? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Just outside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium in vacuum, the normal field is sigma/epsilon_0 and the tangential field is zero. The normal is chosen outward from the conductor, so signed sigma determines field direction.
required_concepts: Normal conductor field sigma/epsilon_0 with zero tangential field.
major_error_concepts: Using the isolated-sheet half-field formula at a conductor boundary without accounting for its zero interior field.

cards.prompt: What is Conducting Cavity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A closed cavity in a conductor at electrostatic equilibrium shields its interior from external electrostatic fields when no charge is inside the cavity. Charges placed inside induce surface charge and generally create a cavity field, so the empty-cavity condition matters.
required_concepts: Empty closed conducting cavity is externally electrostatically shielded.
Internal charges change the conclusion.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the field must vanish inside a cavity even when it contains a charge.

cards.prompt: What is Grounding? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Grounding connects a conductor to a charge reservoir that fixes a chosen reference potential through charge exchange. Grounded means specified potential, not necessarily zero net charge on the object.
required_concepts: Charge exchange fixes reference potential.
Grounded does not imply neutral.
major_error_concepts: Equating zero potential with zero total charge in every geometry.

cards.prompt: What is Capacitance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Capacitance relates separated charge magnitude to potential difference, C=Q/Delta V for a linear two-conductor capacitor. It depends on geometry and dielectric environment rather than on charge alone in the ideal linear model.
required_concepts: Charge-to-voltage ratio for stated capacitor.
major_error_concepts: Assuming doubling Q at unchanged geometry necessarily doubles C rather than voltage.

cards.prompt: What is Parallel-Plate Capacitance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ideal vacuum parallel-plate capacitor has C=epsilon_0 A/d when plate separation is small compared with lateral dimensions and fringe effects are neglected. Charge accumulates with opposite signs on the facing conductors.
required_concepts: Parallel-plate capacitance epsilon_0 A/d.
Neglect fringing under appropriate geometry.
major_error_concepts: Using the formula unchanged when edge effects dominate the geometry.

cards.prompt: What is Series Capacitors? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Ideal capacitors in series carry equal-magnitude incremental stored charge when intermediate nodes have the usual neutral initial condition. Their voltage differences add, giving 1/C_eq=sum 1/C_i for the standard series combination.
required_concepts: Reciprocal capacitances add in series.
Intermediate-node charge assumptions stated.
major_error_concepts: Adding capacitances directly for a simple series connection.

cards.prompt: What is Parallel Capacitors? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Capacitors in parallel share the same voltage across their terminals, while stored charges add. Their equivalent capacitance is the sum of the individual capacitances in the linear ideal model.
required_concepts: Common voltage and additive capacitance.
major_error_concepts: Assuming parallel capacitors must carry equal charges when their capacitances differ.

cards.prompt: What is Capacitor Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The energy stored in a linear capacitor is U=one-half C V squared=Q squared/(2C)=one-half QV. Changes in capacitance require distinguishing fixed charge from fixed voltage because an attached source can exchange energy.
required_concepts: Correct equivalent capacitor energy expressions.
Boundary condition on charge or voltage matters.
major_error_concepts: Using QV without the one-half factor for energy stored by charging a linear capacitor from zero.

cards.prompt: What is Electric Energy Density? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In vacuum the electric-field energy density is u_E=one-half epsilon_0 E squared. Integrating it over space gives field energy where finite; ideal point-charge self-energies require separate care.
required_concepts: Vacuum electric energy per volume proportional to E squared.
major_error_concepts: Using a volume energy density as total energy without integrating or multiplying by volume.

cards.prompt: What is Dielectric Permittivity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A linear isotropic dielectric has permittivity epsilon relating its macroscopic response to electric fields under the model. Filling an ideal plate capacitor increases capacitance by the relative permittivity, but field changes depend on whether charge or voltage is fixed.
required_concepts: Permittivity characterizes linear dielectric response.
Fixed-charge and fixed-voltage cases differ.
major_error_concepts: Claiming inserting a dielectric always reduces voltage even when an ideal source holds voltage fixed.

cards.prompt: What is Polarization? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Polarization P is electric dipole moment per unit volume in a material. It describes the collective displacement or alignment of bound charges, rather than necessarily a transport current of free charges across the material.
required_concepts: Dipole moment density.
major_error_concepts: Equating polarization with free charges continuously flowing through an ideal insulator.

cards.prompt: What is Bound Charge? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Polarization creates bound volume charge rho_b=-divergence P and surface charge sigma_b=P dot n at a material boundary under the standard macroscopic description. Uniform polarization can have no bulk bound charge while still producing surface charge.
required_concepts: Bound volume and surface charge from polarization.
Uniform P can create surface charge.
major_error_concepts: Assuming zero divergence of P implies no bound charge anywhere, including boundaries.

cards.prompt: What is Electric Displacement? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Electric displacement is D=epsilon_0 E+P in macroscopic SI electromagnetism. In a linear isotropic medium D=epsilon E, but the general definition does not assume that simple constitutive law.
required_concepts: D combines vacuum field and polarization.
major_error_concepts: Assuming D=epsilon E with one scalar epsilon for every material and response regime.

cards.prompt: What is Gauss Law for Displacement? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The macroscopic Gauss law for D gives closed displacement flux equal to enclosed free charge. Bound-charge effects are included through P in D, so replacing free charge with all charge double-counts the polarization contribution.
required_concepts: Closed D flux equals free enclosed charge.
major_error_concepts: Using total free-plus-bound charge on the right while retaining the definition D=epsilon_0 E+P.

cards.prompt: What is Electric Boundary Conditions? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Across an electrostatic interface, tangential E is continuous, while the jump in normal E equals total surface charge divided by epsilon_0. Equivalently the normal jump in D tracks free surface charge in the macroscopic description, with a consistent normal convention.
required_concepts: Tangential E continuity and normal jump tied to surface charge.
major_error_concepts: Requiring the normal E component to be continuous across an arbitrary charged surface.

cards.prompt: What is Electric Current? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Electric current is the rate of signed charge crossing a specified surface, I=dQ/dt. Conventional current follows positive-charge flow, opposite the drift direction of electrons in an ordinary metal.
required_concepts: Charge flow rate and conventional positive direction.
major_error_concepts: Assuming electron drift and conventional current necessarily have the same direction.

cards.prompt: What is Current Density? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Current density J is local charge flow per area as a vector, with current through a surface I=integral J dot n dA. For one carrier species in a simple drift model, J=n q v_d.
required_concepts: Vector charge flux density.
Surface integral gives current.
major_error_concepts: Multiplying current density magnitude by arbitrary area without considering orientation or nonuniformity.

cards.prompt: What is Charge Continuity Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Local charge conservation is partial rho/partial t+divergence J=0. Net outward current reduces charge stored inside a region, linking local densities to whole-system charge accounting.
required_concepts: Continuity equation with opposite storage and outflow changes.
major_error_concepts: Claiming nonzero divergence of J is impossible even while local charge is accumulating.

cards.prompt: What is Drift Velocity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Drift velocity is the average carrier motion associated with an applied field, distinct from rapid random microscopic motion. Electrical signals and energy transfer through a circuit need not travel at the slow carrier drift speed.
required_concepts: Average directed carrier velocity.
Not the same as signal propagation speed.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a lamp waits for one electron to drift all the way from the source before responding.

cards.prompt: What is Local Ohm Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For an ohmic isotropic material in its applicable regime, J=sigma_c E, where sigma_c is conductivity. This proportional constitutive relation can depend on temperature and conditions and is not a universal law for every device.
required_concepts: Local linear conductivity relation in a stated regime.
major_error_concepts: Assuming all materials and devices have a constant field-independent conductivity.

cards.prompt: What is Resistance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Resistance relates terminal voltage to current as V=IR for an ohmic element under stated conditions. It is a circuit property distinct from material resistivity and can depend on geometry and temperature.
required_concepts: Terminal voltage-current proportionality for an ohmic element.
major_error_concepts: Treating every nonlinear device as having one constant resistance for all voltages.

cards.prompt: What is Resistivity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a uniform ohmic wire of length L and cross-sectional area A, R=rho_e L/A, where rho_e is electrical resistivity. Resistivity is inverse conductivity in the scalar model and must not be confused with charge or mass density.
required_concepts: Resistance from resistivity times length divided by area.
major_error_concepts: Using charge density in place of electrical resistivity because both are sometimes denoted rho.

cards.prompt: What is Series Resistors? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Ideal resistors in series carry the same current, and their voltage drops add. Their equivalent resistance is the sum of the individual resistances when no extra branch changes the current path.
required_concepts: Common series current and additive resistances.
major_error_concepts: Assuming series components have equal voltage drops despite different resistances.

cards.prompt: What is Parallel Resistors? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Ideal resistors in parallel share a terminal voltage, while currents add. Their equivalent conductance is the sum of conductances, or 1/R_eq=sum 1/R_i for positive resistances.
required_concepts: Common voltage and reciprocal resistance addition.
major_error_concepts: Adding resistances directly for a simple parallel network.

cards.prompt: What is Resistive Power? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ohmic resistor dissipates power P=IV=I squared R=V squared/R. These forms assume the passive sign convention and the stated ohmic relation; dissipated energy accumulates over time.
required_concepts: Equivalent resistor power formulas.
Power differs from energy.
major_error_concepts: Reporting I squared R as energy without a time interval or integration.

cards.prompt: What is Electromotive Force? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Electromotive force is energy supplied per unit charge around a source or circuit-driving process. Despite its name it has units of voltage, and it need not equal the terminal voltage of a loaded nonideal source.
required_concepts: Energy supplied per charge, not mechanical force.
major_error_concepts: Giving EMF units of newtons or equating it automatically with every loaded terminal voltage.

cards.prompt: What is Internal Resistance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A simple source model combines an ideal EMF with internal resistance. While delivering current in that model, terminal voltage is EMF minus the internal resistive drop; charging or reversed current changes the signed relation.
required_concepts: Source internal drop changes loaded terminal voltage.
major_error_concepts: Assuming terminal voltage always equals EMF regardless of current or internal resistance.

cards.prompt: What is Kirchhoff Current Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Kirchhoff's current law states that currents entering and leaving a circuit node balance when charge accumulation there is negligible. More generally their imbalance equals the node's charge accumulation rate.
required_concepts: Node current balance with storage assumption.
major_error_concepts: Using exact zero current sum while excluding a node's significant charge-storage term.

cards.prompt: What is Kirchhoff Voltage Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Kirchhoff's voltage law balances voltage rises and drops around a lumped loop under an appropriate quasistatic circuit description. Time-varying linked magnetic flux must be included through induced EMF rather than ignored as though the electric field were everywhere conservative.
required_concepts: Loop voltage accounting with induction handled explicitly.
major_error_concepts: Applying zero electrostatic circulation around a changing magnetic flux without an induced term.

cards.prompt: What is RC Circuit? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An RC circuit combines resistive dissipation with capacitor charge storage. Its transient follows a first-order equation because capacitor current is C dV_C/dt for constant capacitance.
required_concepts: Resistor-capacitor first-order storage dynamics.
major_error_concepts: Assuming capacitor voltage can jump instantly under a finite current and fixed finite capacitance.

cards.prompt: What is RC Time Constant? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The time constant of a simple single-mode RC circuit is tau=R C for the resistance seen by the capacitor in the stated configuration. It sets exponential relaxation, not the exact finite time at which the transient becomes mathematically zero.
required_concepts: RC exponential timescale.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the exponential transient is exactly zero after one time constant.

cards.prompt: What is Capacitor Charging? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An initially uncharged capacitor connected to a constant ideal voltage through resistance approaches that voltage as V_C=V_source(1-exp(-t/RC)). Its charging current starts largest and decays under the simple circuit assumptions.
required_concepts: Exponential approach to source voltage from zero initial charge.
major_error_concepts: Using the zero-initial-charge formula unchanged for an arbitrary precharged capacitor.

cards.prompt: What is Capacitor Discharging? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A capacitor discharging through a resistor has V_C(t)=V_0 exp(-t/RC) in the ideal simple loop. Its stored energy decays with the square of the voltage and is dissipated in the resistor when no other energy path is included.
required_concepts: Exponential voltage decay and resistive energy transfer.
major_error_concepts: Using the voltage decay factor unchanged for stored energy without squaring it.

cards.prompt: What is Magnetic Field? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A magnetic field B is the vector field entering the velocity-dependent magnetic force q v cross B. Its direction is not defined as the force direction on a stationary charge, which experiences no magnetic force from B alone.
required_concepts: Field determining velocity-cross-field force.
major_error_concepts: Defining B as force per charge on a stationary test charge.

cards.prompt: What is Lorentz Force? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The Lorentz force on a point charge is F=q(E+v cross B) in the classical model. The magnetic contribution changes sign with charge and depends on velocity relative to the chosen inertial frame.
required_concepts: Electric plus velocity-cross-magnetic contributions.
major_error_concepts: Using v dot B as the magnetic force vector.

cards.prompt: What is Magnetic Force and Work? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The magnetic force on a point charge is perpendicular to its instantaneous velocity, so its direct power F_B dot v is zero. Magnetic interactions can still accompany energy transfer through electric fields, constraints, or other system components.
required_concepts: Magnetic part does no direct work on a point charge.
major_error_concepts: Concluding no energy exchange can occur anywhere in a system that contains a magnetic field.

cards.prompt: What is Uniform Magnetic Circular Motion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A charged particle moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field follows a circular path in the nonrelativistic ideal case, with radius m v/(|q|B). Its angular frequency magnitude is |q|B/m and the charge sign controls the rotation direction.
required_concepts: Circular radius and cyclotron frequency under perpendicular uniform-field assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Using the signed charge to produce a negative physical radius.

cards.prompt: What is Helical Magnetic Motion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In a uniform magnetic field with no electric field, a particle's parallel velocity stays constant while its perpendicular velocity rotates. Their combination gives a helical trajectory unless one component vanishes.
required_concepts: Parallel uniform motion plus perpendicular circular motion.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the magnetic force changes the parallel speed in this ideal uniform-field case.

cards.prompt: What is Magnetic Force on a Wire? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The magnetic force on a thin current element is dF=I dl cross B for the appropriate steady-current model. For a straight segment in uniform B it becomes I L cross B, where L follows conventional current.
required_concepts: Current-direction cross-product force.
major_error_concepts: Ignoring the angle between wire current and magnetic field.

cards.prompt: What is Current-Loop Torque? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A planar current loop in a uniform magnetic field experiences torque tau=mu cross B, where mu=I A n follows the right-hand current convention. Its net force is zero in a uniform field, though torque may be nonzero.
required_concepts: Loop torque from magnetic moment cross field.
major_error_concepts: Assuming zero net force rules out a torque on a loop.

cards.prompt: What is Magnetic Dipole Moment? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The magnetic dipole moment of a small planar current loop is mu=I A n. In a prescribed external field its orientation energy is U=-mu dot B for a fixed moment, with force possible in nonuniform fields.
required_concepts: Current-area moment and fixed-moment orientation energy.
major_error_concepts: Defining loop magnetic moment without specifying the current orientation.

cards.prompt: What is Biot-Savart Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The Biot-Savart law gives the magnetostatic field contribution dB=(mu_0/4pi)I dl cross R_hat/R squared for a thin steady current. The source-to-observer vector and cross-product order determine its direction.
required_concepts: Steady-current field integral with dl cross source-observer direction.
major_error_concepts: Applying the steady-current formula as an exact instantaneous law for arbitrary rapidly changing sources.

cards.prompt: What is Long-Wire Magnetic Field? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ideal infinite straight wire carrying steady current has magnetic field magnitude mu_0 I/(2pi r) circling the wire. The direction follows the right-hand rule relative to conventional current.
required_concepts: Circular inverse-distance field around a long straight current.
major_error_concepts: Pointing the field radially away from the wire as if it were an electric line-charge field.

cards.prompt: What is Circular-Loop Field? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: At the center of a circular thin loop of radius R carrying steady current I, the magnetic field magnitude is mu_0 I/(2R). The field points along the loop's normal according to the current's right-hand orientation.
required_concepts: Center-of-loop field and normal direction.
major_error_concepts: Applying the center-field formula unchanged at every off-axis location.

cards.prompt: What is Ampere Circuital Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In magnetostatics, the circulation of B around a closed curve equals mu_0 times the signed steady current through a spanning surface. Symmetry is needed to extract a simple field value from the circulation integral.
required_concepts: Closed B circulation equals mu_0 enclosed steady current.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a constant B magnitude along any chosen loop without a symmetry argument.

cards.prompt: What is Solenoid Field? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Inside an ideal long solenoid in vacuum, the field is approximately uniform with magnitude mu_0 n I, where n is turns per unit length. End effects and external fields are neglected in the long-solenoid approximation.
required_concepts: Long-solenoid field mu_0 n I.
End effects excluded.
major_error_concepts: Using total turn count in place of turns per length without dividing by length.

cards.prompt: What is Toroid Field? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ideal tightly wound toroid with N turns has an approximately azimuthal interior field B=mu_0 N I/(2pi r) in vacuum. It is not exactly constant across a thick toroidal cross section because the radius varies.
required_concepts: Toroid field inversely proportional to azimuthal radius.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the ideal field is uniform across arbitrary radial thickness.

cards.prompt: What is No Magnetic Monopoles? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Classical electromagnetism without magnetic monopoles assigns zero net magnetic flux through every closed surface. Magnetic field lines have no isolated source or sink in this model, unlike electric field lines from charge.
required_concepts: Zero closed magnetic flux under the no-monopole law.
accepted_variants: Absence of isolated magnetic poles in the classical model.
major_error_concepts: Claiming zero net magnetic flux means B must be zero everywhere on a closed surface.

cards.prompt: What is Limits of Magnetostatic Ampere Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The magnetostatic Ampere law alone is incomplete for changing electric fields. Maxwell's additional electric-flux term makes the circulation relation compatible with charge conservation, including charging-capacitor situations.
required_concepts: Time-varying electric field requires displacement contribution.
major_error_concepts: Applying a conduction-current-only loop law to every changing-field configuration.

cards.prompt: What is Magnetic Flux? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Magnetic flux is Phi_B=integral B dot n dA through a specified oriented surface. It can change because the field, area, or orientation changes, and it is not simply B times area unless the geometry supports that simplification.
required_concepts: Oriented normal magnetic-field integral.
major_error_concepts: Ignoring orientation or nonuniformity when replacing flux by B A.

cards.prompt: What is Faraday Induction Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Faraday's induction law relates the oriented EMF around a circuit to the negative rate of change of linked magnetic flux, with the moving-circuit interpretation handled consistently. A changing flux can arise from changing B or moving geometry.
required_concepts: Induced EMF equals negative flux-change rate.
Orientation and circuit motion matter.
major_error_concepts: Restricting induction to changing field magnitude while ignoring changing area or orientation.

cards.prompt: What is Lenz Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Lenz's law gives the direction of induced response: it opposes the change in magnetic flux that produces it under the passive circuit interpretation. It opposes a change, not necessarily the original field itself.
required_concepts: Induction opposes the producing flux change.
major_error_concepts: Claiming induced fields always oppose the existing B even when that existing field is decreasing.

cards.prompt: What is Motional EMF? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Motional EMF arises when charges in a moving conductor experience q v cross B. Around a moving circuit, the relevant force-per-charge integral includes both electric and motion-induced magnetic terms with the chosen circuit velocity.
required_concepts: Conductor motion produces magnetic force per charge.
major_error_concepts: Attributing all motional EMF to a changing B at a fixed location when B can be steady.

cards.prompt: What is Moving-Rod EMF? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A straight rod of length l moving perpendicular to both its length and a uniform magnetic field has ideal motional EMF magnitude B l v. More general orientation requires the integral of (v cross B) dot dl rather than this simple product.
required_concepts: Blv under mutually perpendicular geometry.
major_error_concepts: Using Blv unchanged when the rod moves parallel to B.

cards.prompt: What is Induced Electric Field? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A time-varying magnetic flux produces an electric field with nonzero closed-loop circulation. Such a field cannot be described globally by a single electrostatic scalar potential alone, even though generalized potentials can describe it.
required_concepts: Induced electric circulation differs from electrostatics.
major_error_concepts: Assuming E always equals minus a time-independent scalar gradient in every electromagnetic situation.

cards.prompt: What is Self-Inductance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Self-inductance relates a circuit's own current to its linked magnetic flux in a linear fixed-geometry model, lambda_flux=L I. The resulting induced EMF opposes current change; nonlinear magnetic materials can make a constant L inadequate.
required_concepts: Current-to-flux-linkage coefficient for a linear circuit.
major_error_concepts: Confusing total flux linkage with flux through one turn when many turns link the same flux.

cards.prompt: What is Inductor Voltage? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For an ideal linear inductor under the passive terminal convention, v_L=L dI/dt. The induced source EMF is oppositely signed in Faraday's convention, so terminal voltage and induced EMF labels must be kept consistent.
required_concepts: Passive inductor voltage equals L times current rate.
major_error_concepts: Confusing passive terminal voltage with the negative self-induced EMF without specifying orientation.

cards.prompt: What is Inductor Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A linear inductor stores magnetic energy U=one-half L I squared. Its ideal current cannot jump under a finite applied voltage, because that would require an impulsive current derivative.
required_concepts: Magnetic stored energy and continuous-current implication.
major_error_concepts: Using LI as energy or assuming arbitrary instantaneous current jumps with bounded voltage.

cards.prompt: What is Magnetic Energy Density? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In vacuum the magnetic-field energy density is u_B=B squared/(2mu_0). Energy-density formulas in materials require the appropriate constitutive and reversibility assumptions rather than blindly replacing constants in every nonlinear medium.
required_concepts: Vacuum magnetic energy per volume.
major_error_concepts: Applying the linear vacuum energy formula unchanged to every hysteretic material without accounting for material response.

cards.prompt: What is Mutual Inductance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Mutual inductance relates current in one circuit to flux linkage in another under a linear fixed-geometry model. A changing source current induces a voltage in the other circuit, with sign determined by winding orientation and reference directions.
required_concepts: Cross-circuit current-to-flux-linkage coupling.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the induced voltage has a universal sign independent of winding orientation.

cards.prompt: What is RL Transient? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A simple series RL circuit has current relaxation time tau=L/R. After a DC source step, current approaches its steady value exponentially because inductance resists rapid current change while resistance dissipates energy.
required_concepts: RL timescale L/R and exponential current response.
major_error_concepts: Using RC as the time constant of a circuit containing only R and L.

cards.prompt: What is LC Oscillation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ideal lossless LC circuit exchanges energy between capacitor electric storage and inductor magnetic storage. Its natural angular frequency is 1/sqrt(LC), with amplitude fixed by initial energy in the ideal model.
required_concepts: Electric-magnetic energy exchange with omega_0=1/sqrt(LC).
major_error_concepts: Assuming a lossless LC oscillator decays despite having no modeled loss path.

cards.prompt: What is RLC Circuit? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A series RLC circuit combines oscillatory storage with resistive damping. Its charge equation has L q double prime+R q prime+q/C equal to the source voltage, linking circuit behavior to a forced damped oscillator.
required_concepts: Second-order charge equation with inductive, resistive, and capacitive terms.
major_error_concepts: Assigning the resistance term to q rather than q prime in the stated series charge equation.

cards.prompt: What is Sinusoidal Alternating Current? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Sinusoidal alternating current changes sign periodically and is described by amplitude, angular frequency, and phase. The sinusoidal steady-state model excludes switching transients and does not cover every nonsinusoidal AC waveform with one phasor.
required_concepts: Periodic signed sinusoid with amplitude, frequency, and phase.
major_error_concepts: Assuming any alternating waveform has the same single-frequency phasor representation.

cards.prompt: What is RMS Current and Voltage? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The RMS value is the square root of the time average of the squared signal. For a sinusoid it equals peak magnitude divided by sqrt(2), making resistor average power I_rms squared R in steady conditions.
required_concepts: Root-mean-square definition and sinusoidal peak conversion.
major_error_concepts: Using peak divided by two rather than square root of two for a sinusoidal RMS value.

cards.prompt: What is Circuit Phasor? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An AC phasor is a complex amplitude representing a sinusoidal variable at a fixed frequency under a stated time convention. Circuit equations then use complex algebra while the physical signal is recovered as the corresponding real oscillation.
required_concepts: Fixed-frequency complex amplitude with consistent convention.
major_error_concepts: Combining different frequencies in one phasor equation as though they shared the same time factor.

cards.prompt: What is Inductive Reactance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Inductive reactance magnitude is X_L=omega L. For an ideal inductor under the usual sinusoidal convention, voltage leads current by a quarter cycle, and reactance grows with frequency.
required_concepts: Reactance omega L and voltage lead.
major_error_concepts: Claiming an ideal inductor's reactance decreases as frequency rises.

cards.prompt: What is Capacitive Reactance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Capacitive reactance magnitude is X_C=1/(omega C). For an ideal capacitor, current leads voltage by a quarter cycle, and reactance decreases with increasing frequency.
required_concepts: Reactance inverse to omega C and current lead.
major_error_concepts: Treating a capacitor as a steady DC short after its ideal charging transient has ended.

cards.prompt: What is Impedance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Impedance is the complex phasor ratio Z=V/I at a stated frequency. Its real part describes resistive behavior in a passive simple element, while its imaginary part represents reactive phase response under the chosen convention.
required_concepts: Complex voltage-to-current ratio.
Phase information retained.
major_error_concepts: Adding reactance magnitudes as ordinary positive resistances while ignoring phase.

cards.prompt: What is Series RLC Impedance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a series RLC circuit using exp(i omega t), Z=R+i(omega L-1/(omega C)). The impedance magnitude is sqrt(R squared+(omega L-1/(omega C)) squared), so opposite reactances can cancel.
required_concepts: Series resistive and signed reactive sum.
major_error_concepts: Adding inductive and capacitive reactance magnitudes instead of their signed difference.

cards.prompt: What is Series Circuit Resonance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In the ideal series RLC steady-state model, impedance is purely resistive at omega=1/sqrt(LC). Current then peaks for fixed source-voltage amplitude and constant R, though other circuit observables or topologies can have different resonance peaks.
required_concepts: Series reactance cancellation at LC frequency.
Resonance observable and topology specified.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every circuit voltage and current peaks at the same frequency in all topologies.

cards.prompt: What is AC Power Factor? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Average sinusoidal power is V_rms I_rms cos phi, where phi is the phase difference between voltage and current. The power factor cos phi distinguishes real energy transfer from reactive storage exchange in the simple sinusoidal case.
required_concepts: Average power includes voltage-current phase factor.
accepted_variants: Real AC power and power factor.
major_error_concepts: Equating V_rms I_rms with real average power for arbitrary reactive phase.

cards.prompt: What is Ideal Transformer? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ideal transformer couples changing magnetic flux between windings, giving voltage ratio equal to turn ratio under its assumptions. With lossless transfer, current magnitudes scale inversely, and the ideal ratio does not imply voltage transformation from an unchanging DC flux.
required_concepts: Turn-ratio voltage and inverse current relation in ideal AC coupling.
major_error_concepts: Assuming an ideal transformer continuously transforms a steady DC voltage after all flux changes stop.

cards.prompt: What is Eddy Currents? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Eddy currents are circulating currents induced within extended conductors by changing magnetic flux or motion through appropriate field patterns. Their magnetic effects oppose the producing change, while resistance can dissipate mechanical or field-supplied energy as heat.
required_concepts: Induced bulk current loops with Lenz-law response.
major_error_concepts: Assuming eddy-current heating creates energy without a driving source.

cards.prompt: What is Displacement Current? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In vacuum Maxwell's displacement-current term is epsilon_0 times the time derivative of electric flux in the integral Ampere-Maxwell law. It contributes even where conduction charge does not cross the surface, as between ideal capacitor plates.
required_concepts: Electric-flux change supplies Ampere-Maxwell contribution.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting displacement current as requiring electrons to cross the insulating capacitor gap.

cards.prompt: What is Local Electric Gauss Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The differential electric Gauss law in vacuum is divergence E=rho/epsilon_0, where rho includes all charge. It is the local source form of the closed-flux law under the relevant field or distributional interpretation.
required_concepts: Local electric divergence equals total charge density divided by epsilon_0.
major_error_concepts: Using only free charge with E while omitting bound charge without switching to D.

cards.prompt: What is Local Magnetic Gauss Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The magnetic Gauss law is divergence B=0 in classical electromagnetism without monopoles. It constrains the field's local source structure and is equivalent to zero closed magnetic flux under appropriate regularity.
required_concepts: Zero magnetic divergence.
major_error_concepts: Confusing zero divergence with zero curl or zero magnetic field.

cards.prompt: What is Local Faraday Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The local Faraday law is curl E=-partial B/partial t. It describes electric circulation from a changing magnetic field in fixed spatial coordinates, with the minus sign consistent with oriented induction.
required_concepts: Electric curl equals negative magnetic time derivative.
major_error_concepts: Setting curl E to zero in every time-varying electromagnetic problem.

cards.prompt: What is Ampere-Maxwell Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The vacuum Ampere-Maxwell law is curl B=mu_0 J+mu_0 epsilon_0 partial E/partial t. The conduction and electric-field-change terms together make it compatible with local charge conservation.
required_concepts: Magnetic curl includes conduction and displacement contributions.
major_error_concepts: Omitting the electric time-derivative term in a general vacuum changing-field problem.

cards.prompt: What is Electromagnetic Wave? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In a source-free vacuum region, Maxwell's equations imply wave equations for E and B. Time-varying electric and magnetic fields form propagating coupled solutions without requiring an ordinary material medium.
required_concepts: Source-free Maxwell equations support coupled field waves.
major_error_concepts: Assuming electromagnetic waves require air or a material elastic medium.

cards.prompt: What is Electromagnetic Wave Speed? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The vacuum electromagnetic wave speed is c=1/sqrt(mu_0 epsilon_0). In simple linear media, propagation also depends on constitutive response and can be frequency-dependent, so the vacuum formula should not be applied blindly to materials.
required_concepts: Vacuum speed from electromagnetic constants.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every material wave travels at the vacuum speed regardless of response.

cards.prompt: What is Electromagnetic Transversality? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a source-free plane electromagnetic wave in vacuum, E and B are perpendicular to propagation and to each other. This transverse plane-wave statement does not characterize every near field or arbitrary superposition pointwise.
required_concepts: Plane vacuum wave fields transverse and mutually perpendicular.
major_error_concepts: Assuming arbitrary static or near electric and magnetic fields must always be perpendicular.

cards.prompt: What is Electric-Magnetic Wave Relation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A single traveling plane wave in vacuum has electric and magnetic magnitudes related by E=c B. The cross product E cross B points in its energy-flow direction, with relative signs fixed by the propagation orientation.
required_concepts: E=cB for a vacuum traveling plane wave.
major_error_concepts: Applying E=cB to arbitrary unrelated electrostatic and magnetostatic fields.

cards.prompt: What is Poynting Vector? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The vacuum Poynting vector is S=(1/mu_0)E cross B and represents electromagnetic energy flux. Its time average gives intensity for a steady wave, while local energy-flow patterns can be more complex than one traveling ray.
required_concepts: Energy flux from E cross B divided by mu_0.
major_error_concepts: Treating the Poynting vector as energy per volume rather than power per area.

cards.prompt: What is Poynting Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Poynting's theorem balances changing electromagnetic energy density with outward field-energy flux and work on charges: partial u/partial t+divergence S=-J dot E in vacuum. It connects field energy to material energy transfer.
required_concepts: Field storage plus flux equals negative electrical work rate.
major_error_concepts: Claiming J dot E disappears from energy accounting in a resistive conductor.

cards.prompt: What is Radiation Pressure? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A wave carries momentum as well as energy. At normal incidence in vacuum, ideal absorption gives radiation pressure I/c and perfect reflection gives 2I/c under the stated steady-beam assumptions.
required_concepts: Radiation pressure depends on absorption or reflection.
major_error_concepts: Using the same pressure for ideal absorption and ideal reflection at normal incidence.

cards.prompt: What is Magnetic Boundary Conditions? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Across an interface, the normal component of B is continuous under the no-monopole law. Tangential magnetic-field jumps are tied to surface current, with the macroscopic H formulation separating free current from material magnetization.
required_concepts: Normal B continuity and current-related tangential jump.
major_error_concepts: Demanding all components of B be continuous across any surface-current sheet.

cards.prompt: What is Magnetization? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Magnetization M is magnetic dipole moment per unit volume in a material. The macroscopic auxiliary field H is defined through B=mu_0(H+M), separating applied-current accounting from material response under standard conventions.
required_concepts: Magnetic moment density and B-H-M relation.
major_error_concepts: Equating B and H numerically or dimensionally without the constitutive relation.

cards.prompt: What is Diamagnetism? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Diamagnetic response induces magnetization opposing the applied magnetic field in the simple weak-field description. It does not require permanent magnetic dipoles aligned before the field is applied.
required_concepts: Induced opposing magnetization.
major_error_concepts: Assuming diamagnetism means the material has no electromagnetic response at all.

cards.prompt: What is Paramagnetism? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Paramagnetic response tends to align available magnetic moments with an applied field, producing a positive weak-field susceptibility in the simple model. Thermal disorder competes with alignment, and the response is distinct from spontaneous ferromagnetic order.
required_concepts: Field-favoring alignment of moments without ordinary spontaneous ferromagnetic order.
major_error_concepts: Equating every positive susceptibility with permanent ferromagnetism.

cards.prompt: What is Ferromagnetism? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Ferromagnetic materials can develop spontaneous magnetic order through collective interactions below an appropriate ordering temperature. Macroscopic magnetization also depends on domains and history, so a sample need not present maximal external magnetization without preparation.
required_concepts: Collective spontaneous ordering and domain-dependent bulk response.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every ferromagnetic sample always has a single fully aligned macroscopic domain.

cards.prompt: What is Magnetic Domains? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Magnetic domains are regions with approximately aligned magnetization within an ordered material. Changing external conditions can move domain boundaries or rotate magnetization, altering the net sample moment without requiring every microscopic moment to vanish initially.
required_concepts: Locally aligned regions whose arrangement affects net moment.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting zero net magnetization as proof that all local ordered moments are zero.

cards.prompt: What is Magnetic Hysteresis? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Magnetic hysteresis means magnetization or flux response depends on the history of applied field, not just its current value. A hysteresis loop can represent remanence, coercive response, and energy dissipation over a cycle under appropriate definitions.
required_concepts: History-dependent magnetic response.
major_error_concepts: Using one constant permeability to fully describe a hysteretic cycle.

cards.prompt: What is Conduction and Displacement Current? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Conduction current transports charge, while displacement-current density represents time variation of the electric displacement field in macroscopic Maxwell equations. Both contribute to magnetic circulation, but they describe different mechanisms and may coexist.
required_concepts: Charge transport versus changing displacement field.
major_error_concepts: Assuming displacement current necessarily deposits transported free charge across an insulating gap.

cards.prompt: What is Lumped-Circuit Approximation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A lumped-circuit approximation treats component voltages and currents without resolving appreciable wave-propagation delay across the circuit. It is most appropriate when circuit dimensions are small relative to relevant wavelengths and omitted field couplings are negligible.
required_concepts: Negligible spatial propagation delay and controlled field coupling.
major_error_concepts: Assuming circuit loop rules with ideal lumped elements fully describe arbitrary high-frequency long-wire propagation.

cards.prompt: What is Capacitor Charging Energy Balance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Charging an initially empty capacitor from an ideal constant voltage V through a resistor draws energy C V squared from the source, stores one-half C V squared, and dissipates the other half in the ideal simple charging process. Different driving protocols can change the dissipation.
required_concepts: Source work splits into stored and dissipated energy for the stated process.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the one-half dissipation fraction is unavoidable for every possible charging protocol.

cards.prompt: What is Ideal Circuit Measurements? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ideal voltmeter has infinite input resistance so it draws no current, while an ideal ammeter has zero resistance so it adds no voltage drop. Real meters can load a circuit, and their model must match the quantity being measured.
required_concepts: Ideal nonloading voltage and current meter limits.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every real measurement leaves the circuit unchanged regardless of instrument impedance.

description: A definition-recall course deck covering core concepts in Electricity and Magnetism I.
